_meta.title: Defense Evasion
_meta.description: The art of not being seen: process injection flavors, AMSI/ETW tampering, syscalls, and living off the land. Taught here inseparably from its tripwires - a tool that learns a move learns its alarm.

techniques.name: Process Injection (Hollowing / APC / Thread Hijack)
techniques.summary: Write code into another process's memory and execute it there: hollow a legitimate process's image (replace entry content), queue APC to an alertable thread, or hijack thread context. Runs under a trusted binary's identity - the classic pairing with every initial-access payload.

detection.description: Cross-process memory writes (Sysmon EID 8/10, EDR); RWX private regions in unexpected processes; svchost/notepad with writable executable memory; thread start addresses outside the loaded image; parent-child anomalies.
mitigations: EDR behavioral coverage (injection telemetry beats signature), Sysmon EID 8/10 baseline
CFG / XFG, arbitrary code guard on browsers
Block credential-theft-relevant processes from injection via exploit protection

techniques.name: AMSI Bypass
techniques.summary: Patch the amsi!AmsiScanBuffer return value or the provider's_dll!_CanLoad branch so script content is scanned-and-forgiven. Standard prelude to any PowerShell/JS tradecraft; every red team course teaches the current variant. Short lifecycle per bypass - each known patch gets blocked and a new one is found.

detection.description: Access to amsi.dll memory from managed processes (ETW), EDR hooks on VirtualProtect targeting amsi.dll, PowerShell transcription logging surviving (bypass does not disable transcription), module-unhook signals; block known patch byte-patterns at EDR.
mitigations: PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + transcription + script-block logging (all three)
EDR/AMSI tamper telemetry (patch attempts are themselves high-signal)
Latest .NET/AMSI updates; don't rely on AMSI alone as a control

techniques.name: ETW Patching & Log Tampering
techniques.summary: Patch the EtwEventWrite provider registration or clear logs (wevtutil cl, audit policy flips, timestomping with $FILE_NAME vs $STANDARD_INFORMATION mismatch). Blinding telemetry is the tell that the operator expects to do worse things next - treat as force-multiplier alert, not noise.

detection.description: EtwEventWrite patch attempts (EDR kernel callbacks), log-clear EIDs (1102, 104), audit policy change EIDs (4719), timestomping detection ($SI/$FN delta via NTFS analysis), service/telemetry process termination by unexpected callers.
mitigations: Forward logs off-host in near-real-time (the only real answer to local clearing)
Tamper-protected EDR (self-protection), protected event log (RFC 5849-style wrapping)
Alert on any 1102/104/4719 - these should be rare organizational events

techniques.name: Direct Syscalls & Unhooking (ntdll Refresh)
techniques.summary: Skip hooked user-land APIs entirely: resolve syscall numbers (SSN) from a clean ntdll copy (mapped fresh from disk or the KnownDlls section) or via Hell's Gate/Halo's Gate, then issue syscalls directly - EDR user-mode hooks never see the traffic. This is the modern baseline for offensive tooling and the reason userland hooking alone is not a defense.

detection.description: Kernel-side telemetry is the counter: ETW Ti provider, minifilter file events, syscall anomalies (direct syscalls still hit kernel callbacks), memory regions with RWX and executable syscalls, indirect-syscall stack-spoofing artifacts (return address outside loaded images).
mitigations: Assume userland hooks fail; invest in kernel telemetry + behavioral analytics
Call-stack analysis for return addresses outside known images
Flow-based rather than API-based detections (e.g. 'a process read LSASS memory', regardless of API used)

techniques.name: Living Off the Land (Signed Binary Proxy Execution)
techniques.summary: Abuse signed native tools as proxies: rundll32 executing export ordinals, mshta rendering remote HTA, regsvr32 /i:http, InstallUtil, msbuild inline-task builds, bitsadmin/certutil for transfer. No malware on disk - the LOLBins are the malware, and LOLBas/GTFOBins catalog them exhaustively.

detection.description: Command-line analytics (Sysmon EID 1): office/document apps spawning LOLBins, LOLBins with network URLs in arguments, rundll32 without .dll arguments, mshta spawning children; netconn anomalies (EID 3) from binaries that never legitimately call out.
mitigations: Block LOLB in document/browser context via ASR rules
WDAC allowlisting makes unsigned-argument abuse moot on hardened fleets
Command-line audit + Sigma coverage on the standard abuse arguments
